item.title: "Not negotiating": Trump says "something will happen fairly soon" with Iran, as US mulls fresh strikes
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and that "something" will happen "fairly soon," in an interview with NewsNation White House ...
item.content:encoded:
"Not negotiating": Trump says "something will happen fairly soon" with Iran, as US mulls fresh strikes US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and that "something" will happen "fairly soon," in an interview with NewsNation White House correspondent Libbey Dean. ANI | Updated: 22-10-2026 09:58 IST | Created: 22-10-2026 09:58 IST

US President Donald Trump (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and "something" will happen "fairly soon," Speaking to American news network 'NewsNation's White House correspondent Libbey Dean, Trump was asked about developments in negotiations with Tehran, Trump initially acknowledged some activity but indicated that the outcome remained uncertain. “A little bit, but we'll see what happens,” Trump said when asked whether negotiations with Iran were ongoing. Asked whether he was done negotiating with the Iranian government, Trump said, "No, I think we're not negotiating...we are going to have something, one way or the other. It'll happen fairly soon." He added that some people expected developments to take place after the US election, saying, "Most people think, seem to think it's after the election, and we're going to see what happens." Trump also praised his administration's approach towards Iran, stating, “But I will say this: what we've done with Iran is amazing.” In the interview, Trump also highlighted the situation between Washington and Tehran as "a little conflict against Iran" and said the United States was performing well on both military and economic fronts. "I think our sanctions ended the real deal over there. But we're doing very well militarily and financially against Iran," he said. Trump did not specify what action or development he expected to take place “fairly soon” or provide a definitive timeline for the next steps in the US approach towards Iran. But this comes amid the report by The New York Times that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the American midterm elections, while Tehran has threatened to unveil a weapon it calls the "father of all bombs" amid escalating tensions in West Asia. According to The New York Times, the US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for a short but intensive operation targeting Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations, the report said the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including flying aircraft over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres. US War Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss potential renewed strikes, according to the news report. Some US officials believe another round of "attacks" could push Iran’s economy to the brink and force Tehran to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict. Amid the possibility of renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any renewed military action. According to Iranian state-affiliated media outlet Student News Network (SNN), Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said, "The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them." But, Tehran has not provided details about the weapon or clarified what the threat entails. The warning follows reports that US President Donald Trump has considered using the 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), known as the "Mother of All Bombs", against Iran’s deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility. According to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November, including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces. Officials have cited political considerations, including Trump’s earlier pledge not to strike Iran before the midterm elections, as reasons the operation could be delayed. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, has highlighted the situation as a major challenge for Tehran. In an address to the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, "The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world." He added, "We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm." Iran’s representative to the United Nations also alleged, as cited by the SNN, that "Starlink has been used to identify and target in military attacks against Iran...The country's space and scientific infrastructure has been targeted in attacks." The New York Times report said Washington was seeking to use the prospect of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and control over the Strait of Hormuz. However, Iranian negotiators have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that the matter be deferred until later in the talks. As military preparations and diplomatic efforts continue, the possibility of renewed strikes has raised concerns about a wider regional conflict, with uncertainty persisting over Trump’s final decision and Iran’s potential response. (ANI)

item.title: Quad leaders' summit expected next month, says Rubio as US seeks to revive grouping
item.description: The United States is looking to breathe fresh life into the Quad partnership with India, Japan and Australia, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming that the grouping’s first leaders’ ...
item.content:encoded:
Quad leaders' summit expected next month, says Rubio as US seeks to revive grouping The United States is looking to breathe fresh life into the Quad partnership with India, Japan and Australia, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming that the grouping’s first leaders’ summit in more than two years is expected to take place next month during Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-related meetings in Manila, according to US media reports. ANI | Updated: 22-10-2026 09:43 IST | Created: 22-10-2026 09:43 IST

From left, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pose following a Quad ministerial meeting at Hyderabad House in New Delhi. (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The United States is looking to breathe fresh life into the Quad partnership with India, Japan and Australia, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming that the grouping’s first leaders’ summit in more than two years is expected to take place next month during Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-related meetings in Manila, according to US media reports. Rubio told an Indian News network that an agreement had been reached to hold the summit during the meetings scheduled in Manila from November 15 to 17, although a specific date had not yet been finalised. “We don’t have the specific date yet, but that’s going to happen, and we’re very enthusiastic about it,” Rubio said. According to US media, Rubio has been a strong supporter of the Quad, which brings together India, the United States, Japan and Australia. The grouping was conceived by former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in 2007 to bring together four like-minded democracies. The proposed summit would be the first Quad leaders’ meeting since September 2024, when Joe Biden was US President. Rubio met his counterparts from the three partner countries a day after the inauguration of President Donald Trump’s administration and has since participated in two further meetings of Quad foreign ministers, the latest in July. However, Trump has yet to participate in a Quad leaders’ meeting during his current presidency, raising concerns among officials in Tokyo, Canberra and New Delhi about the grouping’s direction under his administration. As per the Japanese media, Trump has appeared more focused on high-profile bilateral engagements, including meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing and Washington this year. Trump also said this week that he was open to holding a trilateral summit with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin focused on “denuclearisation”, potentially on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit scheduled in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. The proposed summit could help address concerns that the grouping has lost momentum under Trump’s administration. However, Japanese media say the long-term effectiveness of the partnership would depend on whether its members could translate diplomatic engagement into concrete outcomes. Rubio has argued that the grouping is increasingly moving beyond ministerial discussions towards practical cooperation in areas such as critical minerals, emerging technologies, maritime security and energy security. "The Quad is not just a process by which we meet and agree to do certain things," Rubio said on Tuesday. "You are now starting to see action; you are now starting to see things happen. And that’s what we’re excited about for the leaders’ meeting, is that at that meeting they will be able to actually announce concrete actions, not just simply a nice social gathering, but something that has concrete deliverables." Nevertheless, as per the Japanese media, questions remain over whether the four countries can maintain the degree of strategic alignment achieved during the Biden administration, particularly following Trump’s tariff disputes with India, Japan and Australia and his efforts to strengthen ties with Beijing. Meanwhile, Japan, Australia and India have been working to deepen their bilateral partnerships, according to the news report, as they seek to reinforce cooperation amid uncertainty over the Quad’s direction. The proposed summit comes as Rubio concluded his visit to India on October 21, following engagements in Mumbai. His visit took place amid efforts by New Delhi and Washington to strengthen their strategic partnership, advance negotiations on a proposed bilateral trade agreement and expand energy cooperation. In Mumbai, Rubio held talks with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on the India-US strategic partnership and progress in negotiations on the proposed trade deal. He also paid floral tributes to the victims of the November 2008 Mumbai terror attacks, which claimed the lives of six American nationals. Energy cooperation has emerged as an important component of the broader bilateral relationship, with discussions encompassing energy trade, India’s imports of Russian petroleum and opportunities to expand purchases of American energy resources. The visit also drew attention to potential investment by Reliance Industries in a new petroleum processing facility in the United States. US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor had highlighted the prospective project in the context of efforts to increase domestic energy production and generate employment. Rubio’s India visit and the proposed Quad leaders’ summit underline Washington’s engagement with New Delhi on strategic and economic issues. (ANI)

item.title: Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
item.description: Read more about Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff on Devdiscourse ...
item.content:encoded:
Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff Reuters | Updated: 21-10-2026 23:59 IST | Created: 21-10-2026 23:59 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Wednesday and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step toward ending the war in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue toward planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and called the Russian leader a "humanitarian", in footage of the exchange, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Putin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said Putin had freed Hubbard at the request of US President Donald Trump, and had also taken into account the American's poor health. "The president sends his thanks, our whole nation sends their thanks, because of Stephen Hubbard," Witkoff told Putin in a meeting shown on state TV. "Because of you he's going home to his family." A video shared with Reuters showed Witkoff and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev meeting Hubbard, who wore a dark fleece and was clean-shaven, in an undisclosed location. He shook Witkoff's hand and said: "Thank you very much for all your efforts." Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, told Reuters in a voice message that he spoke briefly by phone with his father before he boarded the airplane in Russia. "Today he seemed light in his step, a sense of happiness in his voice", Coleman said. THREE-WAY MEETING PLANNED ON WAR Witkoff called the talks with Putin "constructive" and said in a post on X that he had also met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo to advance Trump's mission to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, who met Witkoff, told public broadcaster NRK that the agreement to hold another "high-level tripartite meeting" between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv will likely happen in mid-November and focus on a potential post-conflict security structure. Witkoff's praise for Putin over Hubbard's release was scorned by some in Washington. Republican US Senator Thom Tillis said in an X post directed at the US envoy: "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say." In a statement, Hubbard's US-based lawyer, Martin De Luca, thanked Trump, Witkoff and other US officials for securing Hubbard's release, calling it "a dividend earned along the hard road to peace". Trump said in a Truth Social post that the US had not been required to give anything in return for the release. "The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin," the post said. "Welcome home Stephen, it's great to have you back," wrote Trump, who later also posted a picture of Hubbard appearing inside a plane with others and holding an American flag. FAMILY, LAWYER DISPUTED CONVICTION Hubbard, a native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence of six years and 10 months in Russia following a conviction for mercenary activity in a closed-door trial. He was arrested in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, where Russian prosecutors alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges. But De Luca previously told Reuters that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. In a 2024 interview with Reuters, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, also disputed the idea that her brother took up arms for any government, calling him "so non-military" and pointing out his advanced age. As of Wednesday, Hubbard was the only US prisoner held by Russia who was designated by Washington as "wrongfully detained". The Trump administration secured the release last year of another American jailed in Russia, schoolteacher Marc Fogel, who had been serving a 14-year prison term for drug smuggling.
